tagline: Country loops link glacial lakes, wooded parks and a surviving watermill.
intro: The Glacial Ridge Trail Scenic Byway follows several country loops between Willmar and Glenwood, with extensions to Alexandria and Sauk Centre. Explore Minnesota identifies it as an officially designated Minnesota State Scenic Byway and describes rolling terrain with lakes, woods, prairie and farmland. Sibley, Monson Lake and Glacial Lakes state parks bring hardwood forest and water into the journey. This is a route with loops and side trips, rather than a single end-to-end road.

Glaciers left the hills and lakes that define the route. At Monson Lake, detached blocks of ice melted where they lay, forming three kettle lakes. Later park building created places to visit this terrain, with stone structures and a gravel entrance road. Civilian Conservation Corps workers built Sibley’s stone structures in 1935–38. At Monson Lake, a veterans’ corps built with local granite and white oak while Works Progress Administration crews made the gravel entrance road and parking lot.

One journey starts at Alexandria and reaches Glenwood on Lake Minnewaska before continuing toward Sunburg and Monson Lake. The southern loops take in Willmar and New London, near Sibley State Park. Terrace adds a mill on the East Branch of the Chippewa River, and the network extends onward to Sauk Centre.

moments.title: Monson Lake State Park
moments.text: Three kettle lakes occupy much of Monson Lake State Park, with islands and narrow strips of land between them. Detached glacier ice melted here, leaving the basins. The park also preserves a difficult human history. It began as a memorial to 13 Swedish American settlers killed during the Dakota War of 1862. Treaty violations by the United States and late or unfair annuity payments had caused hunger and hardship among the Dakota. The Monson Lake Memorial Association created a private park in 1927. Memorial observances initially presented only the settlers’ perspective; injustices suffered by the Dakota entered the programming in 1987.

moments.title: Sibley State Park
moments.text: Rustic stone buildings give Sibley State Park a visible connection to the Civilian Conservation Corps. Crews constructed them between 1935 and 1938 beside Andrew Lake, near New London. The park’s layout reduced congestion and overcrowding for swimmers, picnickers and campers. The stone structures are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. They make the park’s history of planned recreation legible alongside its lake and woodland setting.

moments.title: Terrace Mill
moments.text: The flour mill that began work here in 1870 did not stay. In the mid-1890s it moved to Brooten to be nearer a new railroad line. Jonas M. Danelz bought the property in 1901 and built the present Terrace Mill in 1903. Later owners added diesel power, then turned the mill into a woodworking shop making church furniture after grist milling ended in 1949. Preservation began in the 1970s, and the mill now operates as a museum. Its historic district includes the dam and a stone arch bridge from 1903, preserving the components of a rural water-powered milling complex.
moments.notice: The mill complex includes a 1903 stone arch bridge and a mill dam.
